raw_text:
### Introduction
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge, characterized by high morbidity, recurrent hospitalizations, and poor long-term survival rates [26]. Over the last decade, the pharmacotherapy of HF has undergone a radical shift, primarily driven by the introduction of angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs). Sacubitril/valsartan is a first-in-class ARNI that delivers dual therapeutic action. It combines sacubitril, a prodrug that inhibits neprilysin (an enzyme responsible for degrading beneficial vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin), with valsartan, an angiotensin II type 1 ($AT_1$) receptor blocker. This dual mechanism enhances the protective cardiovascular and renal effects of the natriuretic peptide system while simultaneously suppressing the maladaptive renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) activation.

### Clinical Evidence in HFrEF
The clinical efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan in HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) was firmly established in the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial [1]. In this double-blind trial of 8,442 ambulatory patients with HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan demonstrated a 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization compared to the active control enalapril [1]. Beyond this primary outcome, ARNI therapy showed superior efficacy in halting clinical disease progression [15], reducing the incidence of sudden cardiac death [16], and improving patient-reported health-related quality of life [17]. These therapeutic benefits were consistently observed across various baseline patient profiles, including different ages [25] and across the range of background medication doses [22]. Mechanistically, trials like PROVE-HF and EVALUATE-HF demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan therapy promotes significant reverse cardiac remodeling, leading to sustained reductions in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels, improvements in left ventricular size, and reductions in aortic stiffness [5, 6].

### In-Hospital Initiation and Advanced Disease
To explore safety in acute settings, the PIONEER-HF and TRANSITION trials evaluated early initiation of ARNI [2, 4]. PIONEER-HF showed that initiating sacubitril/valsartan in patients hospitalized for acute decompensated HF, once hemodynamically stabilized, led to a significantly greater reduction in NT-proBNP and a 42% reduction in clinical rehospitalizations compared to enalapril [2]. TRANSITION further demonstrated that in-hospital or early post-discharge initiation is safe and clinically feasible, irrespective of prior ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy [4], a finding supported by the TITAN study which verified dose titration safety [20].

However, the benefits of ARNI have limitations in certain patient cohorts. In advanced, end-stage HFrEF, the LIFE trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan did not offer a statistically significant advantage over valsartan alone in reducing NT-proBNP or cardiovascular outcomes, suggesting limited efficacy in advanced mechanical or transplant-eligible cohorts [13]. Similarly, the PARADISE-MI trial evaluated sacubitril/valsartan in the acute post-myocardial infarction setting and did not find a significant reduction in composite CV death or incident HF compared to the ACE inhibitor ramipril [12].

### HFpEF and HFmrEF Spectrum
Extending the treatment paradigm to HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) was evaluated in the PARAGON-HF trial [3]. Although sacubitril/valsartan narrowly missed statistical significance for the overall primary endpoint compared to valsartan (relative risk reduction of 13%, p=0.059) [3], subsequent prespecified analyses revealed significant clinical benefits in specific subgroups. Females [11] and patients with lower-range ejection fractions (up to 57%) derived substantial benefit from the therapy, showing significant reductions in HF hospitalizations. A pooled analysis of the PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF trials confirmed that the therapeutic benefit of sacubitril/valsartan extends well into the mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) range, showing treatment efficacy that begins to decline only as left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) exceeds 55–60% [9]. Quality of life improvements [29] and reduced hospitalizations were particularly pronounced in those with a recent HF hospitalization [30].

### Extracardiac Benefits and Safety
Beyond primary cardiac endpoints, sacubitril/valsartan possesses crucial secondary benefits. Renal outcome analyses in the PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF trials revealed a slower rate of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline and a lower risk of renal failure in patients receiving the ARNI compared to enalapril or valsartan [10, 18, 19], a protective effect corroborated by the UK HARP-III study in non-HF chronic kidney disease [28]. Additionally, initiating sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a lower rate of severe hyperkalemia when combined with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [27] and led to improved long-term glycemic control in patients with comorbid diabetes mellitus [23].

### Current Guidelines and Future Directions
Based on this extensive body of evidence, current international guidelines strongly endorse sacubitril/valsartan. The 2021 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines [8] and the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines [7] recommend ARNI as a Class I, Level of Evidence A therapy for HFrEF, prioritizing it as a first-line agent or as a replacement for ACE inhibitors/ARBs. For HFmrEF and HFpEF with below-normal LVEF, both guidelines offer weaker but supportive recommendations (Class IIa/IIb) [7, 8]. Looking forward, pediatric trials like PANORAMA-HF have expanded its use to younger cohorts [21], while health-economic evaluations confirm its long-term cost-effectiveness [24]. Estimations of lifetime benefits project that comprehensive therapy including ARNI can add up to several years of additional life expectancy compared to conventional regimens [14].
